name: Road network (routing graph)
plain: A compact map of Puerto Rico's drivable roads, stored as junctions and the road pieces between them. The route planner uses it to follow streets. The file itself is not drawn on the map; transit route lines that follow streets are drawn from it.
definition: A directed graph built from OpenStreetMap roads: junctions (including points where a long road piece was cut), road pieces (edges) and interior bend points. A divided road has one road piece for each direction, so total length counts both directions. Each road piece stores its two end junctions, its length in 2 m steps, a road class code (0 to 14), a one-way flag and the number of bend points between its ends.
unit: Counts of junctions, road pieces and bend points; lengths in metres (stored in 2 m steps); coordinates in steps of 0.00001 degree (about 1.1 m)
geography: Main island of Puerto Rico, Vieques and Culebra (separate pieces of the graph). Mona Island has no roads in the file

coverage.frequency: Rebuilt only when the road network is rebuilt from a new OpenStreetMap extract, not on a fixed schedule. The nightly transit refresh reads the file but does not change it

method: roads.py reads the Geofabrik Puerto Rico extract of OpenStreetMap, keeps drivable roads (see the entry on which roads are kept), cuts them into pieces at junctions, drops bend points within about 2 m of a straight line, and writes the binary file.
source_detail: OpenStreetMap highway ways from the Geofabrik Puerto Rico extract (puerto-rico-latest.osm.pbf), data timestamp 2026-10-01T20:22:06Z, read with the osmium library
how_to_read: Use it to see which streets a route can follow. It is not a full road inventory: it holds drivable roads only, as volunteers mapped them. Do not use it to measure total road length or road condition. In the 2026-10 snapshot the file holds 193,507 junctions, 226,421 road pieces and 536,209 bend points. The pieces add up to about 33,100 km, counting both directions of a divided road. The file is 6,409,964 bytes. The OpenStreetMap extract it was built from has a data timestamp of 2026-10-01 20:22 UTC (Coordinated Universal Time; Puerto Rico is 4 hours behind).
caveats: Left out: service roads (driveways, parking aisles, alleys), tracks, footpaths, cycle paths and roads tagged private, no access, no motor vehicles or no vehicles (unless tagged for buses). Some real streets are therefore absent.

A road that is missing or wrongly tagged in OpenStreetMap is missing or wrong here. The data reflect the extract of 2026-10-01. The file itself does not record that date; it was read from the extract's header.
In the 2026-10 snapshot the graph has 363 separate pieces. The largest holds 98.8% of the junctions. Vieques and Culebra are separate pieces, so a route cannot follow roads between islands.
The file has no turn bans, tolls, traffic signals, road surface, lane counts or traffic.

License: Open Database License (ODbL) 1.0. Credit line: Data © OpenStreetMap contributors, available under the Open Database License (ODbL). Read the terms at openstreetmap.org/copyright before reusing the data.

values.header (20 bytes): The letters PRRD, then four whole numbers: version (1), number of junctions, number of road pieces, number of bend points. All numbers are little-endian (the lowest byte comes first).
values.nodes: One pair of whole numbers per junction: x = (longitude + 68) x 100,000 and y = (latitude - 17) x 100,000. One step is 0.00001 degree, about 1.1 m.
values.edges: One 12-byte record per road piece: start junction, end junction, length in steps of 2 m (up to 65,535), a flag byte (bits 0 to 3 are the road class, bit 4 is set when the piece is one-way from start to end) and the number of bend points between its ends (0 to 250).
values.shape: The bend points of every road piece in order, each stored as a small step (dx, dy) from the previous point, in the same 0.00001 degree units.

name: Road class and planning speed
plain: Every road piece has a class code from 0 to 14, taken from OpenStreetMap, and each class has a planning speed. The router uses the speeds to pick the fastest road and to estimate time.
definition: The road class is stored in the low four bits of each road piece's flag byte. The planning speed is a fixed number of kilometres per hour for each class, set in roads.py and repeated in the same order in roads.js.
unit: Class code (0 to 14); planning speed in kilometres per hour
geography: Main island of Puerto Rico, Vieques and Culebra (separate pieces of the graph). Mona Island has no roads in the file

coverage.frequency: Rebuilt only when the road network is rebuilt from a new OpenStreetMap extract, not on a fixed schedule. The nightly transit refresh reads the file but does not change it

method: The class is the OpenStreetMap highway value of the road. The speeds are planning values set in the code, not measured. Only the ratios between classes decide which road is the fastest choice; the absolute values set the estimated time.
source_detail: OpenStreetMap highway tag; speeds from roads.py (SPEED_KMH) and site/js/roads.js
how_to_read: Read '90' as 'the router treats this class as 90 km/h', not as a speed limit. The router picks the path with the least travel time at these speeds, so it prefers faster road classes but still avoids long detours. The class comes from OpenStreetMap. The speeds are planning values chosen by Foundation for Puerto Rico (FPR) in the observatory's code. They are not OpenStreetMap data, so do not credit them to OpenStreetMap.
caveats: Planning speeds are not speed limits, observed speeds or bus speeds.
The class comes from volunteers' tags in OpenStreetMap. It can differ from a road's official class or its PR route number.

Kilometres add up the length of every road piece. A divided road is mapped as two one-way pieces, one for each direction, so both are counted: the motorway total is the length of both carriageways added together, not the length of the road itself. It is not lane-kilometres.
Class 13 (service) exists in the code but no road piece carries it.

name: Which OpenStreetMap roads are kept
plain: The road network keeps roads that cars and buses can drive. It leaves out driveways, parking aisles, footpaths and roads closed to motor vehicles.
definition: A way in OpenStreetMap is kept when its highway tag is one of 14 values (motorway, trunk, primary, secondary, tertiary, their link ramps, unclassified, residential, living_street and busway) and no access tag closes it to motor vehicles. Every other way is dropped, including highway=service.
geography: Main island of Puerto Rico, Vieques and Culebra (separate pieces of the graph). Mona Island has no roads in the file

coverage.frequency: Rebuilt only when the road network is rebuilt from a new OpenStreetMap extract, not on a fixed schedule. The nightly transit refresh reads the file but does not change it

method: 1. Keep ways whose highway tag is one of the 14 classes. 2. Drop a way tagged access=no or access=private, motor_vehicle=no or vehicle=no, unless it is tagged bus=yes or bus=designated. 3. Set direction: oneway=yes, true or 1 means one-way along the way; oneway=-1 or reverse means one-way against it; oneway=no means two-way. With no oneway tag, only motorways, motorway ramps and roundabouts are one-way. 4. A point becomes a junction where two or more ways meet, or where a way starts or ends. The part of a way between two junctions is a road piece. A piece that starts and ends at the same junction with no bend points is dropped. 5. Drop bend points within about 2 m of a straight line to the end of the piece. Cut a piece with more than 250 bend points into several pieces. 6. Measure each piece along its bends and store its length in 2 m steps.
source_detail: roads.py (_usable, _read_ways, _finish, write_bin)
how_to_read: Use this entry to see why a street you know cannot be used by the router. It may be a service road, a path, a road under construction or a road tagged private in OpenStreetMap.
caveats: A road tagged access=destination or access=customers is kept.
Roads tagged highway=construction or highway=proposed are not kept.
A oneway=reversible tag is not read. Such a road is treated as two-way unless it is a motorway or a roundabout.
Pedestrian streets are not in the road network. They do appear in the place-name index.

name: How the router follows roads
plain: The planner snaps each point you choose to the nearest road within 500 m, then finds the fastest road path between the points at planning speeds. A leg with no road path is drawn as a straight line.
definition: Fastest path on the road graph, where each road piece costs its length divided by the planning speed of its class. Two-way pieces can be used in both directions; one-way pieces only from start to end. The same method runs in the browser (roads.js, for the route planner) and at build time (roads.py, for drawing published transit routes).
geography: Main island of Puerto Rico, Vieques and Culebra (separate pieces of the graph). Mona Island has no roads in the file

coverage.frequency: Rebuilt only when the road network is rebuilt from a new OpenStreetMap extract, not on a fixed schedule. The nightly transit refresh reads the file but does not change it

method: Snap: each chosen point goes to the nearest point on any road piece within 500 m, by straight-line distance. Search: an A* search (a shortest-path search guided by straight-line distance) finds the fastest path between consecutive points, starting and finishing anywhere along a road piece. Check: a leg counts as 'on roads' only when both points snap and the road path is no longer than 4 times the straight-line distance plus 1,500 m. Otherwise the leg is drawn straight and marked as unable to follow roads.
source_detail: site/js/roads.js (snap, route, path) and roads.py (Roads); parameters used by site/js/plan.js
how_to_read: The drawn line is one plausible road path. A real bus may take another street.
caveats: Snapping uses straight-line distance. A point can be matched to a road on the other side of a river or a fence.
The router has no turn costs, signals or traffic. It picks the fastest path at planning speeds, not the shortest and not the path a bus takes.
The detour limit is a plausibility test. It does not prove that no road connection exists.
A route can have at most 8 points: From, To and up to 6 added stops.

values.Snap radius: 500 m. A point farther than this from every road makes its legs straight lines.
values.Detour limit: A road path longer than 4 times the straight-line distance plus 1,500 m is rejected, and the leg is drawn straight.
values.Gap between a point and its road: The straight-line distance is added to the leg length and counted at walking pace, 1.4 m/s (5 km/h).
values.Leg that cannot follow roads: Drawn straight, length is the straight-line distance, time counted at 8 m/s (28.8 km/h).
values.Planning speeds: 12 to 90 km/h by road class; see the entry on road classes.

view.label: Map, Transit tab, Plan a route (example: Río Piedras to Caguas)

name: How published transit routes are drawn along roads
plain: Some transit feeds give no route shape, so the build joins consecutive stops along the road network. The line then follows streets and does not cut across blocks.
definition: Each published route line carries a geometry source. A route with a shape in the feed keeps it ('shape'). A route without one is drawn along roads between its stops ('roads'; 'roads_inferred' when the feed lists the stops out of order). It is joined by straight lines between stops ('stops') when too few pairs of stops can be snapped (less than 60% in a direction), or when the feed lists the stops out of order and the route has more than 45 distinct stops. Routes that volunteers mapped in OpenStreetMap keep their own lines ('osm').
geography: Routes of every operator in the observatory

coverage.frequency: Redone at each full build and by a nightly transit refresh that finds a changed feed; a route whose stops did not change keeps its earlier line

method: For each pair of consecutive stops: closer than 25 m, keep a two-point line. Otherwise snap both stops to roads within 500 m and find the fastest road path. Accept it when its length is at most 3 times the straight-line distance plus 400 m; if not, that pair stays a straight line. A route counts as road-following when at least 60% of the pairs in each direction snap. When the feed's stop order is not geographic (the path through the stops in listed order is more than 2.5 times longer than a nearest-neighbour tour, or the stops are in alphabetical order), the order of visit is inferred from road travel distances for routes with up to 45 distinct stops. The final line is simplified to about 3 m (0.00003 degree).
source_detail: network.py (snap_routes, RoadSnapper, order_quality) with roads.bin; GTFS means General Transit Feed Specification, the standard format of public timetable feeds
how_to_read: A line on the map that follows streets is an estimate of where the vehicle drives. The exact street may differ from the one drawn. For the number of routes drawn each way in the current snapshot, see the entry on how the route line was drawn.
caveats: The line is an approximate path between stops. The exact street may differ.
Where a feed lists the stops out of order, the order of visit is inferred and the route's times are not used in the timetable replay.
The geometry_source field of the routes file records which of these methods drew each route.

view.label: Map: Transit routes layer (dotted lines join stops with no road path)

values.shape: Line from the operator's own route shape.
values.roads: The feed has no route shape; the line follows roads between the stops in listed order.
values.roads_inferred: The feed lists the stops out of travel order; the order of visit is inferred and the line follows roads.
values.osm: Line mapped by volunteers in OpenStreetMap.
values.stops: Too few pairs of stops could be snapped to roads, or the stops are out of order and the route has more than 45 distinct stops; straight lines join the stops.

name: Place-name index
plain: A list of named places, streets, highway numbers and landmarks (48,450 names in the 2026-10 snapshot), each with a point on the map. The search boxes and the route planner look names up in it, inside your browser.
definition: The file has three parts. 'munis' lists the 78 municipality names in alphabetical order. 'kinds' lists the 19 type codes in a fixed order. 'items' lists the names. Each item is [name, latitude, longitude, kind number, municipality number] with an optional sixth value, a note. The kind number and the municipality number are positions in the 'kinds' and 'munis' lists. Items are sorted by kind, then by name without accents.
unit: Rows of name, point and codes (counts of names); latitude and longitude in decimal degrees rounded to 5 places (about 1 m)
geography: Puerto Rico: 78 municipalities, with places on Vieques, Culebra and Mona Island

coverage.frequency: Rebuilt only when the place-name index is rebuilt, from the OpenStreetMap extract downloaded for the road network; not on a fixed schedule

method: gazetteer.py reads named points and ways from the OpenStreetMap extract, adds the municipality and barrio boundaries from the Census Bureau (TIGERweb generalized 500k, shoreline-clipped), gives each name its municipality by point-in-polygon (checking which boundary contains the point), and writes one compact file. The entries on kinds and on how the index is built give the rules.
source_detail: OpenStreetMap, Geofabrik Puerto Rico extract with data timestamp 2026-10-01T20:22:06Z; municipality boundaries from US Census Bureau TIGERweb Generalized_ACS2023 State_County MapServer layer 11 (Counties 500K) and barrio boundaries from TIGERweb Generalized_ACS2023 Places_CouSub_ConCity_SubMCD MapServer layer 7 (County Subdivisions 500K), both shoreline-clipped (municipios.geojson, barrios.geojson)
how_to_read: The index holds names with one point each. It has no house numbers or postal addresses. It does not hold the tourism listings; the pages search those separately.
caveats: Names are as OpenStreetMap volunteers wrote them. Spelling, capital letters and abbreviations vary.
Only OpenStreetMap points and ways are read. A place mapped only as a multi-part area (a relation) is missing.
Place tags (place=village, hamlet, suburb, neighbourhood, island and so on) are read from points only. A place mapped only as an area (a closed way) is not in the index.

A road name has one row for each municipality that holds the middle point of at least one of its mapped pieces (OpenStreetMap ways). A road mapped as several pieces usually has a row in each municipality it crosses. A single piece that crosses a boundary counts only where its middle point lies, so a long road mapped as one piece has one row.
A road or place that is not mapped with a name in OpenStreetMap is not in the index.

values.munis: List of the 78 municipality names, sorted alphabetically without accents. A row's municipality number is its position in this list, starting at 0.
values.kinds: List of the 19 type codes: municipio, town, village, barrio, neighborhood, road, route, hospital, school, university, civic, transport, park, beach, peak, water, landmark, airport, mall. A row's kind number is its position in this list, starting at 0.
values.items: List of rows [name, latitude, longitude, kind number, municipality number] with an optional note as a sixth value. In the 2026-10 snapshot, 7,506 rows carry a note.

name: Place-name types
plain: Each name in the place-name index has one of 19 types, such as municipality, street, highway number, hospital or beach. The type sets how the name is ranked and labelled in search results.
definition: The kind is a number in each row of the index: its position in the 'kinds' list. The observatory's pages show a plain label for it in search results and rank some types ahead of others (a municipality ahead of a street).
unit: Type code (19 values) and count of names
geography: Puerto Rico: 78 municipalities, with places on Vieques, Culebra and Mona Island

coverage.frequency: Rebuilt only when the place-name index is rebuilt, from the OpenStreetMap extract downloaded for the road network; not on a fixed schedule

method: gazetteer.py assigns the type from OpenStreetMap tags. For a named point it tests place, amenity, natural, historic, aeroway, leisure and shop, in that order. For a named area that is not a road it tests amenity, leisure, natural, aeroway, shop and historic. Roads are ways with a highway tag and a name or a PR route number. The first match wins. Place tags are read from points only. Only OpenStreetMap points and ways are read; the municipality and barrio rows come from Census Bureau boundaries (TIGERweb generalized, 500k, shoreline-clipped).
source_detail: gazetteer.py (KINDS, PLACE_KIND, AMENITY, LEISURE, NATURAL, HISTORIC, ROAD_CLASSES); labels from site/js/plan.js (KIND_INFO); municipality boundaries from US Census Bureau TIGERweb Generalized_ACS2023 State_County MapServer layer 11 (Counties 500K) and barrio boundaries from TIGERweb Generalized_ACS2023 Places_CouSub_ConCity_SubMCD MapServer layer 7 (County Subdivisions 500K), both shoreline-clipped (municipios.geojson, barrios.geojson)
how_to_read: The counts show what OpenStreetMap volunteers have named. A low count can mean that few features exist or that few are mapped with a name. For example, the 2026-10 snapshot has 32 airport rows.
caveats: The types follow OpenStreetMap tags, not official categories. A clinic is filed under 'hospital'; a marina, a bay and an island mapped as a point are filed under 'water'.
Tourism listings (restaurants, hotels, attractions) are not part of this index.
The 'barrio' rows come from Census boundaries, not from OpenStreetMap.

name: How the place-name index is built
plain: The index starts from names in OpenStreetMap and adds Census rows for municipalities and barrios. Each name gets a municipality. A street that is mapped in several pieces lying in different municipalities gets a row in each.
definition: gazetteer.py turns the OpenStreetMap extract and the published boundaries into rows [name, latitude, longitude, kind, municipality, note].
geography: Puerto Rico: 78 municipalities, with places on Vieques, Culebra and Mona Island

coverage.frequency: Rebuilt only when the place-name index is rebuilt, from the OpenStreetMap extract downloaded for the road network; not on a fixed schedule

method: 1. Read OpenStreetMap nodes and ways that have a name and a matching tag. Place tags (town, city, village, hamlet, suburb, neighbourhood, quarter, locality, island, islet) are read from points only. Ways that are not roads are placed at the average of their corner points. 2. Add one row for each municipality and each barrio in the published boundaries. 3. Give each name its municipality by point-in-polygon (checking which boundary contains the point) on the municipality boundaries. A point offshore (a pier or a cay) goes to the nearest municipality when it is within about 2 km (0.02 degree); any other name outside every municipality is dropped. 4. For roads, give each way to the municipality that holds its middle point (the middle mapped point by count of points, not by length). Group ways by name and municipality, place the row at that middle point of the longest piece, and drop street names whose pieces total less than 60 m. A road with a Puerto Rico (PR) route number but no name is also read. Route numbers are taken from the ref tag (the first one, for example PR-52, with an optional letter) and grouped the same way, with the road's local name as the note. Highway numbers are not dropped for length. 5. Drop exact repeats: the same name (ignoring accents and capitals), the same type, and latitude and longitude that are equal when rounded to 3 decimals (cells of about 110 m). 6. Sort by type, then name, round coordinates to 5 decimals and write the file.
source_detail: gazetteer.py (read, main); municipality boundaries from US Census Bureau TIGERweb Generalized_ACS2023 State_County MapServer layer 11 (Counties 500K) and barrio boundaries from TIGERweb Generalized_ACS2023 Places_CouSub_ConCity_SubMCD MapServer layer 7 (County Subdivisions 500K), both shoreline-clipped (municipios.geojson, barrios.geojson)
how_to_read: A road has one point for each municipality in which the middle point of one of its mapped pieces lies, placed at the middle point of its longest piece there, so the point may not be where you expect. In the 2026-10 snapshot the boundaries give 78 municipality rows and 901 barrio rows.
caveats: The index uses the OpenStreetMap 'name' tag only. Alternative names and translations are not read.
Place polygons mapped as relations are not read.
Place tags (town, city, village, hamlet, suburb, neighbourhood, quarter, locality, island, islet) are read from points only. A place mapped only as an area (a closed way) is not in the index.
The note on a place is the OpenStreetMap place type, for example hamlet or suburb. It is not an official classification.

name: How place-name search matches
plain: Search finds names that start with, or contain, the words you type, ignoring accents and capital letters. It also expands common abbreviations in what you type, such as 'av' to 'avenida'.
definition: The search boxes in the header and in the route planner ask the place-name index, in your browser. A typed text is cleaned, optionally read as a highway number or as coordinates, matched to names and ranked.
geography: Puerto Rico: 78 municipalities, with places on Vieques, Culebra and Mona Island

coverage.frequency: Runs in your browser each time you type (about 0.1 second after you stop); uses the index published in the current snapshot

method: 1. Clean the text: remove accents, change to lower case, turn the marks . , ; : ( ) " ' into spaces. 2. If the whole text is pr, ruta, route, carr, carretera, hwy or highway followed by a number of up to 4 digits and an optional letter (for example 'pr 52', 'carr52' or 'highway 52'), it becomes 'pr-52'. Longer text such as 'pr 52 caguas' is not changed this way. 3. Expand words one by one: av, ave, avda to avenida; cll to calle; carr, ctra to carretera; urb to urbanizacion; bo to barrio; res to residencial; hosp to hospital; univ to universidad; pza to plaza; mt to monte. 4. Score each name: 0 exact match; 1 starts with the text; 2 every typed word starts a word of the name; 3 every typed word appears somewhere in the name; no match otherwise. 5. Rank by score, with a small advantage for some types (a municipality ranks ahead of a street); equal scores go to the name nearest the map centre, then to the shorter name. 6. Keep up to 4 rows with the same name and type for streets and highways (6 for other types). The combined list shows at most 12 results, with at most 4 streets, 3 highways, 5 tourism places, 4 stops and 4 of any other type. 7. Two numbers that each have at least two decimals, separated by a comma or a space (for example 18.40, -66.05), are read as latitude and longitude, latitude first. Search starts at 2 characters.
source_detail: site/js/plan.js (parseQuery, textScore, Gaz.search, searchEverything, attachSearch)
how_to_read: Type a part of the name. If a name is stored with an abbreviation, type another word from it. If nothing matches, try fewer words. Names with equal scores are listed nearest to the map centre first, so move the map near the place you want. For a street address, use the online lookup. To search by coordinates, type latitude first, then longitude, each with at least 2 decimals.
caveats: Abbreviations are expanded in what you type, not in the stored names. In the 2026-10 snapshot, 66 stored names contain a word that search expands, such as 'Av.', 'Urb.' or 'Bo.' (for example 'Urb. Marbella'). Typing that word does not find them, because the typed word is expanded and the stored word is not. Typing another word from the name does.
Matching is exact on letters. A misspelling finds nothing.

Online address lookup is optional. It runs only when you choose 'Look up as an address online', which appears after 4 or more characters. It sends the text you typed to the OpenStreetMap Nominatim service, which has its own usage policy. The request also sends your IP address and browser details to the OpenStreetMap server. Nothing else you type leaves the page.
Besides the index, the search boxes also look at the page's own data: tourism places (under the current filters), scheduled stops, stations and terminals, and, in the header box only, transit routes.

name: Build information file (meta.json)
plain: A small file that says when the data snapshot was built, which area it covers, how many records each step kept, and which sources were used. Cite its snapshot label and date.
definition: meta.json has 13 parts: label, generated_at, bbox, counts, sources, housing, landuse, barrios, transport, network, time, taxonomy_dropped_top and access. The full build (build.py) writes all of them. The nightly transit refresh (refresh_network.py) rewrites the 'network' part on nights when it finds a changed feed. Through access.py it also rewrites the 'access' part, and the count places_near_transit inside 'transport', when a value changes.
unit: Mixed: text, dates, coordinates and counts

coverage.frequency: Rewritten at each full build (build.py); the last full build is dated 2026-10-02 UTC

method: build.py collects the sources, classifies and filters the data, writes every data file and then writes meta.json with the label, the time, the settings and the counts of what each step kept.
source_detail: build.py (main) and the SOURCES, meta and counts of transport.py, network.py, housing.py, landuse.py and timeseries.py

name: Duplicate listings folded
plain: How many listings were merged into another listing because they looked like the same place. The observatory keeps the best record of each group.
definition: The number of listings removed by duplicate folding: for each group of listings judged to be the same place, the group size minus one.
geography: Puerto Rico (the map box, see the entry on the map box)
method: Listings are compared only when they have the same category and the same address town (the municipality named in the address, or the nearest municipality centre when the address names none). Two such listings are treated as one place when they are close (within 600 m; within 1,000 m for beaches, parks, nature reserves, scenic areas, historic sites and tourist attractions) and their names are very similar (a match score of at least 0.95, or at least 0.8 when within 150 m or, for those types, 600 m). Listings that share a phone number, have somewhat similar names (at least 0.5) and are within 500 m are also merged. The kept record has the highest confidence, then the most contact details, then the most social links.
source_detail: build.py (dedup, similarity). The separate phone, email and social-media fields are used only while matching duplicates and are not published.
how_to_read: A listing's 'duplicates' value in the places file says how many records it absorbed. In the 2026-10 snapshot, these add up to 1,005.
caveats: The rules can merge two real places with similar names that stand close together, and can miss duplicates with different names.
Folding is done on listings, not on what is physically on the ground.

The method text in the file calls the affordability table Table 6, the number this dictionary and the Housing page use. The study PDF prints that table as Table 8.

The study's printed maximum loans work out at a rate of 4.994%, so using exactly 5% leaves the observatory's figures $19 to $65 below them. It is a modelling assumption, not a mortgage rate in force in any year, and the result is an indicator, not a loan limit and not advice on buying a home.

name: Time-view facts in the build file
plain: Facts for the time views: the number of weekday trips, which weekday the timetable stands for, and how many Atlantic storms passed near Puerto Rico (from 1851 through 2025 in the 2026-10 snapshot).
definition: trips is the weekday trip count at the last full build. trips_day is the label of the timetable day used. The weekday timetable uses each feed's Wednesday service or, if a feed has none, the first of Tuesday, Thursday, Monday or Friday that it serves. storms_near_pr counts Atlantic tropical cyclones whose track came within 250 km of a point at the centre of the island (18.22, -66.45). major_hurricanes_near_pr counts those whose strongest wind near Puerto Rico was category 3 or higher on the Saffir-Simpson scale. storm_years gives the first and last year in the list.
geography: Puerto Rico and its surrounding waters

coverage.frequency: Rewritten at each full build (build.py); the last full build is dated 2026-10-02 UTC. In the 2026-10 snapshot the storms run from 1851 to 2025

method: build.py counts the weekday trips it writes. timeseries.py reads the HURDAT2 best-track database of NOAA (the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration), keeps storms within 250 km of the island's centre and assigns a category from the peak wind (in knots) within that distance: 64 or more category 1, 83 category 2, 96 category 3, 113 category 4, 137 category 5.
source_detail: build.py (meta['time']); timeseries.py (load_hurricanes); HURDAT2 is the National Hurricane Center's Atlantic hurricane database
how_to_read: The storm counts are storms that came near the island, not storms that struck it.
caveats: In the 2026-10 snapshot, trips (3,312) is the weekday trip count written by the last full build. It includes 15 trips on five routes whose stop order is unreliable. A later nightly refresh leaves those routes out, which gives 3,297, the count in the network part of meta.json and in trips.json. Use 3,297 for the timetable replay.
The category is from the wind near Puerto Rico, not the storm's peak anywhere on its track.

Distance and category come from the recorded track points (about every six hours), not from the line between them. A storm whose recorded points were all farther than 250 km is left out even if its path crossed the circle.
250 km is measured from one point at the centre of the island, so a storm can pass nearer the east or west end than the centre and still be left out.

Observation methods changed a great deal between 1851 and 2025. Older tracks and winds are less certain, and the National Hurricane Center (NHC) revises past seasons from time to time, so do not read the counts as a trend by decade.

name: Data inventory (registry.json)
plain: A list of the data files the observatory publishes. For each file it gives the title, the size, the records, fields and values, the dates it was first published and last updated, the dictionary items that document it and the state of its compliance review; for the whole folder, the totals, their history and the counts of what is not published. It does not list registry.json itself. The Data management page, the data dictionary and the Ask the observatory chat read it.
definition: registry.json holds built (the date its content last changed), snapshot (the label of the build), total_bytes, limits, used_fraction, needs_planning, growth_note, totals (the counts of the whole folder), history (the totals on each date they changed), domain_names (the names of the domains in Spanish and English), withheld (the counts of what is not published) and files, one row for each published file except registry.json itself.
unit: Bytes (sizes), a share, a date and text

coverage.frequency: Updated by registry.py at the end of each full build, on each nightly transit refresh and whenever it is run by hand; registry.json is rewritten only when its content changes (its built field gives that date)

method: registry.py calls ledger.py for every published file: ledger.py reads the file, counts its records, fields, values and vertices with the adapter of the file's family (docs/data-management.md) and computes its content hash. registry.py then updates the ledger (dictionary_src/data_ledger.json: the first-published and last-updated dates, the versions and the history of the totals), adds the titles, domains, licence classes, reviews and flags of the data contract (dictionary_src/datasets.json) and the number of dictionary entries that name each file, and writes registry.json only when something other than the date changed. python registry.py --check fails when the ledger or registry.json does not describe the files as they are; it never compares a date with today.
source_detail: registry.py and ledger.py; written by the observatory's own build step, not an external source
how_to_read: Use it to see what the observatory holds, how big each file is and when it changed. The Data management page shows it as a table with totals, a growth chart and the counts of what is not published; the data dictionary summarises it. In the map's Ask the observatory chat, ask 'how big is the database?' to see it summarised.
caveats: A file added after the last registry run is not listed until registry.py runs again; the tests (python registry.py --check) fail until it does.

In a full build the registry is written last, after the dictionary and the catalog, so their sizes are current. catalog.json is written before it, so the weight it gives registry.json is one build behind.
Sizes are the bytes of the files as published, with line ends counted as one byte; a copy checked out on Windows can be larger on disk.
The list shows what is published, not what is planned. Planned data is in the wanted-data list.

name: Records, fields and values (data points) of a published file
plain: How much data a published file holds: its records (the observation units, such as a municipio in a year or a place), its fields (the variables they carry) and its values (the data points: each field of each record that holds a value). Vertices count the positions of its geometry apart. The Data management page shows them for every file, with totals.
definition: A record is an observation unit: a feature of a GeoJSON file; a row of a table (a place, a stop, a trip, a road edge, a census block); in a series file, an area in a period that holds at least one value (a municipio in a year, a barrio in a five-year window). A field is a variable the records carry (a GeoJSON property, a series variable, a margin of error, a column); a cell that holds a list is one field, and in a file with several tables the fields of each table are counted. A value (data point) is a non-null scalar in a field of a record; a list cell counts its non-null elements; null, absent and the empty string are missing. Metadata (titles, labels, notes, sources, build dates, methods, checks), geometry coordinates, the keys a file stores once as a lookup (geo.ids, years) and lookup tables (a legend, the CPI deflator, the gazetteer) are not values. A vertex is a position of a geometry: a GeoJSON coordinate pair, a point's latitude and longitude, a path point, a road node or shape point.
unit: Counts: records, fields, values and vertices

coverage.frequency: Updated by registry.py at the end of each full build, on each nightly transit refresh and whenever it is run by hand; registry.json is rewritten only when its content changes (its built field gives that date)

method: ledger.py reads each published file and applies the adapter of its family: GeoJSON (features and their properties; the positions of the geometry), series (every area and period of geo.ids and the years of each variable and margin of error, with the per-area and island tables of economy_series.json and housing_series.json), columnar files (one list per field, one position per record: the exposure files, place_access.json, wcrp_rvi_inputs.json, wcrp_social.json), lists of records (places.json, transport.json, hurricanes.json, population_blocks.json), and one adapter each for the tables of transit_supply.json, the trips files, operators.json, geo/crosswalk.json, housing.json and landuse_summary.json. roads.bin is read from its header: one record per road edge with three fields (length, road class, one-way), and its nodes and shape points as vertices. Documentation (system.docs) and the place-name index (system.tools) are listed and sized but not counted. The counts of municipalities.json, barrios.geojson, places.json and acs_barrio.json were checked by an independent script (docs/data-management.md).
source_detail: registry.py and ledger.py; written by the observatory's own build step, not an external source
how_to_read: In the file of 2026-10-19 the 60 data files hold 409,574 records, 1,381 fields and 3,520,446 values; roads.bin holds 679,263 of the values (226,421 road edges). A value that two files repeat counts in each, so the total measures what is published, not distinct facts.
caveats: A record is not the same unit in every file: a municipio in a year, a barrio in a window, a place, a trip. Compare records within a family of files.
Coded values such as 99,999 metres (beyond the search limit) count as values; only null, absent and empty text are missing.
The counts of the versions published before 2026-10-19 (the growth history) use today's adapters on the old files.

name: First published and last updated dates of a published file
plain: When a data file first appeared on the published site, and when its content last changed. A rebuild that writes the same data on another day changes neither date, so the dates show when new information was added.
definition: first_published is the date the file first reached the published site; it never moves. last_updated is the last date its content hash changed, and versions the number of content versions published. The content hash is the SHA-256 (its first 16 hexadecimal digits) of the file's JSON in canonical form (keys sorted, no spaces) without the build stamps built, generated_at and snapshot_built outside its records; a file that is not JSON is hashed as bytes. Dates are Puerto Rico dates (UTC-4).

coverage.frequency: Updated by registry.py at the end of each full build, on each nightly transit refresh and whenever it is run by hand; registry.json is rewritten only when its content changes (its built field gives that date)

method: The ledger (dictionary_src/data_ledger.json) keeps each file's dates, versions, hash, size and counts. Up to 2026-10-19 it was rebuilt from git (python ledger.py --backfill): each commit of the first-parent history of main is a publication on its Puerto Rico date; a file's first_published is the date of the first such commit that holds it, and last_updated the date of the last one that changed its content hash. From then on, registry.py compares the hashes at every build: a changed hash sets last_updated to the build date and adds a version; a new file gets both dates; first_published never moves; a rebuild with the same content changes nothing. The nightly transit refresh runs the same step and commits the ledger with the data.
source_detail: registry.py and ledger.py; written by the observatory's own build step, not an external source
how_to_read: On 2026-10-19, flood.geojson was first published on 2026-10-01 and never changed (one version); places.json was first published on 2026-10-01 and last updated on 2026-10-18 (eight versions).
caveats: Before 2026-10-19 a date is the day the change was merged into main, which publishes the site; from then on it is the day of the build that changed the file, which can be a few days before the merge.
Only content counts: a new build date written inside a file is not an update.
catalog.json and the dictionary files change whenever the dictionary or the size of any file changes, so they are updated often.

versions counts each build that changed the content. A branch built several times with different content counts each build; python ledger.py --backfill origin/main followed by python registry.py counts it again from the history of main.

name: Compliance review of a published file
plain: Whether a published file still needs a review before it can be relied on, and why: a review of personal data, of a license or of federal grant content that is still open, one that was cleared and when, a license the sources do not state, or nothing to review.
definition: review.status is open when a review of the file in the data contract (dictionary_src/datasets.json) is open, cleared when every review was cleared, unstated when the file has no review and its licence class is unstated, that is, at least one of its sources states no licence (a file takes the most restrictive licence class of its sources, and review.licence_from names the sources that set it), and none otherwise. review.open lists each open review with its type (pii, licence or compliance) and a short reason in Spanish and English; review.cleared is the latest date a review was cleared. review.flags lists federal-grant (the file holds or describes federal grant money or a grant-funded program), counts-only (sensitive items are counted but not drawn or named), licence-unstated and licensed-not-open.

coverage.frequency: Updated by registry.py at the end of each full build, on each nightly transit refresh and whenever it is run by hand; registry.json is rewritten only when its content changes (its built field gives that date)

method: registry.py reads the reviews, flags and licence class of the file's record in datasets.json. contract.py checks them: a review needs a type, a status and a note; an open review should have a summary and a cleared one a date; a file flagged federal-grant must have a compliance review.
source_detail: registry.py and ledger.py; written by the observatory's own build step, not an external source
how_to_read: On 2026-10-19, 7 reviews are open in 6 files: the names of drawn places (places.json), two license reviews (municipalities.json and housing.json, withdrawn on 2026-11-23 with the figures they covered), federal grant content (housing.json, housing_series.json and economy_series.json) and the terms of HRSA's files (health_series.json). 24 files have a source that states no license, most often the municipal GTFS feeds (15 files); barrios.geojson, for example, takes the class from those feeds alone, while its other sources state a license.
caveats: The status says what the data contract records; it is not a legal opinion.
Federal grant content needs Finance and Compliance review before external communication.

values.cleared: Aprobada / Cleared, with the date of the latest clearance.
values.unstated: Licencia sin declarar / License not stated: no review is open, and at least one source states no license; the cell names it (review.licence_from).
values.federal-grant: Flag: federal grant money or a grant-funded program.
values.counts-only: Flag: sensitive items counted but not drawn or named.
values.licence-unstated: Flag: at least one source states no license (a file takes the most restrictive license class of its sources); the flag names it.
values.licensed-not-open: Flag: a source licensed to FPR whose data need written permission to republish; the flag names it.

name: Data dictionary file (dictionary.json)
plain: The whole data dictionary in one file: every entry, source record and glossary term. The data dictionary page reads smaller files made from it. You can download it and use the dictionary in your own tools.
definition: dictionary.json is a JSON file (a standard text format for structured data) with 12 parts: built, snapshot, snapshot_built, domains, kinds, entries, sources, aliases, id_alias, glossary, domain_info and coverage. 'entries' has one record for each documented dataset, variable, map layer, boundary, category, measure and method. 'sources' has one record for each source of data or software. 'glossary' has one record for each term or abbreviation. The table of codes describes each part.
unit: Text records: entries, sources and glossary terms

coverage.frequency: Rewritten each time the dictionary is built, including at the end of every full build (build.py). The file's 'built' field gives the date.

method: dictionary.py reads the dictionary's entry files, source records and glossary, adds the names, units, years and sources that the economy and housing series catalogs already hold, reports any published data field that has no entry, and writes one compact JSON file with no spaces. Entries are sorted by area, group and name. A second, much smaller file, dictionary_summary.json, holds only the counts that the About tab shows. dictionary.py also writes, from the same content, the files the dictionary page reads (docs/performance.md): dictionary_list.json, read first, with the list, the filters, the sources, the glossary and the words the search looks in; and one file for each top-level domain, dictionary_detail_<domain>.json, with the rest of each entry (the whole summaries, definition, method, how to read it, cautions, codes, related entries and where it appears), which the page fetches the first time an entry of that domain is opened, printed or exported.
source_detail: dictionary.py (build); the entries, sources and glossary written by Foundation for Puerto Rico (FPR); the observatory's own build step, not an external source
how_to_read: Download it to use the dictionary in your own tools. Find an item in 'entries' by its id, which is also the part of the page address after the # sign (for example dictionary.html#roads.network). The ids in an entry's 'sources' list are keys of the 'sources' part. When you cite the file, give its 'snapshot' label and its 'built' date.
caveats: The file describes the data of the snapshot named in 'snapshot'. Its 'built' date can be later than 'snapshot_built', because the dictionary is rebuilt on its own as well as at the end of a full build.
Figures in the entry text (counts, shares, sizes) come from a particular snapshot or file and carry its date. Check the date before you reuse a figure.

Entries describe the observatory's data, not the original sources. Each source keeps its own license and terms. The 'sources' records give the license as the publisher states it, which is not legal advice.
No license is stated for the dictionary text itself. It is FPR work.
dictionary_summary.json is a separate small file with the counts the About tab shows: entries, data sources and glossary terms. It is not a copy of the dictionary.
