geography: Any route in Puerto Rico (calculated for the route you draw)

coverage.frequency: Recalculated in your browser each time the route changes, from the data published in the current snapshot. Resident counts are from the 2020 Census

method: roads.js finds the fastest road path for each leg and measures the drawn line with a flat-earth approximation. plan.js adds the legs. With more than one leg, the card also lists each leg with its length and, for legs on roads, its minutes. The label is 'by road' when every leg follows roads, 'partly by road' when some do not, and 'straight line' when Follow roads is switched off.
source_detail: site/js/roads.js (path) and site/js/plan.js (renderResult); roads.bin from OpenStreetMap
how_to_read: It is the length of the path the planner drew, not a measured distance on the ground. It is not the fastest or shortest real bus route.
caveats: A leg that cannot follow roads, for example a leg to another island, counts at its straight-line length, so it can be much shorter than any real trip by sea or air.
If the road file cannot be loaded, the route is drawn as straight lines and a note under the numbers says so.
In the GeoJSON download the same number is called length_km and has two decimals.
The points you choose are stored in the page address (after #r=) to about 11 m. A shared link shares them. Do not choose a home address if you plan to share the link.
example: Snapshot 2026-10, From Río Piedras (town) To Caguas (municipality): 24.3 km, by road.

view.label: Map, Transit tab, Plan a route (example: Río Piedras to Caguas)

name: Indicative running time
plain: A rough driving time for the route, in minutes, at fixed planning speeds by road class. It leaves out stops, traffic and waiting. Use it to compare routes, not as a bus timetable.
definition: The sum over legs of the time at planning speeds. On a leg that follows roads: the time along each road piece (its length divided by the speed of its road class), plus the straight-line gap between each chosen point and its road, counted at walking pace (1.4 m/s). On a leg that cannot follow roads: its straight-line length at 8 m/s (28.8 km/h). Shown as '~N min', rounded to whole minutes, at least 1.
geography: Any route in Puerto Rico (calculated for the route you draw)

coverage.frequency: Recalculated in your browser each time the route changes, from the data published in the current snapshot. Resident counts are from the 2020 Census

method: roads.js adds the seconds of every leg. plan.js shows the total only when Follow roads is on and at least one leg follows roads; otherwise it shows a dash. In the list of legs, minutes appear only for legs that follow roads.
source_detail: site/js/roads.js (path, SPEED_MS) and site/js/plan.js (renderResult)
how_to_read: The number is the time at these planning speeds, for example 25 km/h on residential streets and 90 km/h on motorways. It is closer to a free-flow driving time than to a bus timetable: in the example (snapshot 2026-10, Río Piedras to Caguas) the average speed is about 76 km/h (24.3 km in about 19 min). A real bus trip is longer: it has stops, boarding, signals and traffic. Use the number only to compare routes.
caveats: The speeds are planning values by road class, not observed or posted speeds.
When some legs cannot follow roads, the total time still includes them, as straight lines at 8 m/s (28.8 km/h). The list of legs shows minutes only for legs that follow roads.
The time is not a prediction of a real service and does not depend on the day or the hour.
example: Snapshot 2026-10, From Río Piedras (town) To Caguas (municipality): about 19 min for 24.3 km.

view.label: Map, Transit tab, Plan a route (example: Río Piedras to Caguas)

name: Residents within 400 m of the route
plain: How many people live in census blocks whose point is within 400 metres of the planned route. It shows who lives near the line, not who would ride it.
definition: The sum of the 2020 Census resident counts of every census block with residents whose internal point lies within 400 m (straight line) of the route line. A block counts whole when its point qualifies. Blocks are not split.
geography: Census blocks of Puerto Rico (36,570 blocks have residents in the 2020 Census)

coverage.frequency: Recalculated in your browser each time the route changes, from the data published in the current snapshot. Resident counts are from the 2020 Census

method: population_blocks.json lists, for every block with residents, its longitude and latitude (the Census internal point, rounded to 4 decimals), its residents and its distance to the nearest scheduled stop. plan.js simplifies the route line to a 12 m tolerance and adds the residents of each block whose point is within 400 m of any piece of it.
source_detail: US Census Bureau TIGERweb tigerWMS_Census2020 MapServer layer 10 (2020 Census blocks), fields POP100, INTPTLAT, INTPTLON; site/js/plan.js (score)
how_to_read: Use it as a catchment: the number of people close to the line. It is not ridership or demand.
caveats: The distance is in a straight line, not along streets. A person can be within 400 m and still face a long walk.
A block is counted whole or not at all. A large block whose point is farther than 400 m is left out even if part of it is near.
The counts are from April 2020 and have not been updated.
400 m is about a quarter mile, the walking distance the observatory uses for access to a stop.
example: Snapshot 2026-10, From Río Piedras (town) To Caguas (municipality): 26,723 residents.

view.label: Map, Transit tab, Plan a route (example: Río Piedras to Caguas)

name: Residents within 400 m of the route who have no scheduled stop within 400 m
plain: Of the people who live within 400 m of the route, how many live more than 400 m from every scheduled stop in the observatory's data. These people have no scheduled stop near them.
definition: Residents counted in 'Residents within 400 m of the route' whose census block has its nearest scheduled stop more than 400 m away (straight line). A scheduled stop is a stop in a public timetable feed (GTFS, the General Transit Feed Specification) from ATI (Autoridad de Transporte Integrado) or from a municipal system. The result card calls them 'of them have no scheduled stop within 400 m today'.

coverage.frequency: Recalculated in your browser each time the route changes, from the data published in the current snapshot. Resident counts are from the 2020 Census

method: population_blocks.json gives each block's distance in metres to its nearest scheduled stop, capped at 9,999. plan.js adds the residents of the blocks near the route whose distance is above 400. The distances are recomputed by the transit refresh.
source_detail: population_blocks.json (network.py, coverage); site/js/plan.js (score)
how_to_read: Compare it with 'Residents within 400 m of the route'. A high share means the route passes many people who have no stop nearby today. The distances were last computed on 2026-10-02.
caveats: 'Today' means the build or refresh date. Stops of operators whose timetables have expired still count as stops, so the true number with no service now is larger.
Only stops in public timetable feeds count. Routes that volunteers mapped in OpenStreetMap have no stops here, so público service is not counted as service.
A stop within 400 m says that a stop exists. It does not say how often vehicles come or when.
The distance is in a straight line, not along streets.
example: Snapshot 2026-10, From Río Piedras (town) To Caguas (municipality): 13,301 of the 26,723 residents.

view.label: Map, Transit tab, Plan a route (example: Río Piedras to Caguas)

name: Tourism places within 400 m of the route
plain: How many tourism places lie within 400 m of the planned route, and how many of them are lodgings. Tourism places are Attractions, Gastronomy (restaurants, bars and cafes), Accommodations and Visitor services.
definition: The number of listings in the places file with an Overture confidence of at least 0.5, other than places of worship, whose point lies within 400 m (straight line) of the route line. Lodgings are the places in the Accommodations category (the route card calls them lodgings).
unit: tourism places (listings after duplicate folding); lodgings (a part of them)
geography: Any route in Puerto Rico (calculated for the route you draw)

coverage.frequency: Recalculated in your browser each time the route changes, from the data published in the current snapshot. Resident counts are from the 2020 Census

method: plan.js goes through the places file, skips places of worship and listings below 0.5 confidence, and counts those within 400 m of the simplified route line. It counts the lodgings separately.
source_detail: Overture Maps Places, release 2026-09-23.1, classified by build.py; site/js/plan.js (score)
how_to_read: It says how many visitor places the route passes. A place is a listing, not a verified business.
caveats: The same 0.5 confidence rule as the map statistics applies. The map's own filters (categories, confidence slider) do not change this count.
Listings can be closed, moved or missing.
The distance is in a straight line, not along streets.

Lodgings are listings the observatory's rules file under hotels, resorts, inns, guest houses, hostels, campgrounds and vacation properties (categories such as vacation rental, villa, cottage, cabin, holiday and condo), or under Overture's lodging group. They are Overture listings, not a lodging register.
example: Snapshot 2026-10, From Río Piedras (town) To Caguas (municipality): 400 tourism places, 16 of them lodgings.

view.label: Map, Transit tab, Plan a route (example: Río Piedras to Caguas)

name: Share of the route that runs alongside an existing route
plain: The share of the planned route within 150 m of a published transit route; a high share means the route mostly repeats lines that exist. The card turns amber above 50%, a threshold this tool chose.
definition: The share of the route's sample points that have a published route line within 150 m, rounded to a whole percent. Routes that volunteers mapped only in OpenStreetMap (públicos) and ferry routes are not counted. Routes of every other operator are counted, including the Tren Urbano rail line.
unit: % of sample points along the route
geography: Any route in Puerto Rico (calculated for the route you draw)

coverage.frequency: Recalculated in your browser each time the route changes, from the data published in the current snapshot. Resident counts are from the 2020 Census

method: plan.js indexes every segment of the published route lines in grid cells of 0.002 degree (about 220 m) and tests each sample point against the segments in its own and the neighbouring cells. See the entry on how the route is sampled.
source_detail: transit_routes.geojson (all operators except 'osm' and ferries); site/js/plan.js (segments, score)
how_to_read: 100% means the route follows existing lines for its whole length. 0% means no line from an ATI (Autoridad de Transporte Integrado) or municipal timetable feed is near. Públicos mapped in OpenStreetMap and ferries are not counted. It says nothing about stops or how often vehicles run.
caveats: Lines of operators whose timetables have expired are counted.
A route can run beside a line and still have no stop near it. The measure compares lines, not stops.
It is a share of sample points, not of length. See the entry on sampling.
The 50% amber threshold is this tool's own choice, not a standard.
example: Snapshot 2026-10, From Río Piedras (town) To Caguas (municipality): 100%. From Mayagüez (municipality) To Aguadilla (municipality): 0%.

view.label: Map, Transit tab, Plan a route (example: Río Piedras to Caguas)
Map, Transit tab, Plan a route (example with no overlap: Mayagüez to Aguadilla)

name: Share of the route in a flood hazard area
plain: The share of the planned route that crosses areas the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) maps as high-risk for flooding, which have a 1% chance of flooding in any year. The card turns amber above 20%.
definition: The share of the route's sample points that fall inside a polygon of the National Flood Hazard Layer of FEMA (the Federal Emergency Management Agency) flagged as a Special Flood Hazard Area (SFHA_TF = T), rounded to a whole percent. In the published file these are zones A, AE, AH, AO, A99 and VE. Zone X and zone D are not counted.
unit: % of sample points along the route
geography: Any route in Puerto Rico (calculated for the route you draw)

coverage.frequency: Recalculated in your browser each time the route changes, from the data published in the current snapshot. Resident counts are from the 2020 Census

method: plan.js tests each sample point against the polygons of the flood file with a point-in-polygon test (checking whether the point lies inside the polygon). See the entry on how the route is sampled.
source_detail: FEMA National Flood Hazard Layer, layer 28 (flood.geojson, field SFHA_TF); site/js/plan.js (score)
how_to_read: A high value means much of the route lies in mapped flood hazard. It does not say how deep water would get or whether the road is raised.
caveats: The flood polygons are simplified by about 5 m for display, so points near a boundary can be misplaced.
It is a share of sample points, not of length.
The map shows hazard at a point. It does not describe bridges, culverts or the road surface.
The 20% amber threshold is this tool's own choice, not a standard.
example: Snapshot 2026-10, From Río Piedras (town) To Caguas (municipality): 8%.

view.label: Map, Transit tab, Plan a route (example: Río Piedras to Caguas)

name: Share of the route in protected areas
plain: The share of the planned route that passes through protected areas in the USGS Protected Areas Database. The card shows it only when it is above 0%.
definition: The share of the route's sample points that fall inside any polygon of the protected-areas file (USGS, the United States Geological Survey), rounded to a whole percent. Every designation is counted, including the proclamation boundaries (PROC) such as El Yunque National Forest and the Culebra and Vieques National Wildlife Refuges.
unit: % of sample points along the route
geography: Any route in Puerto Rico (calculated for the route you draw)

coverage.frequency: Recalculated in your browser each time the route changes, from the data published in the current snapshot. Resident counts are from the 2020 Census

method: plan.js tests each sample point against the polygons of the protected-areas file with a point-in-polygon test (checking whether the point lies inside the polygon). See the entry on how the route is sampled.
source_detail: USGS PAD-US 4.1 (protected.geojson); site/js/plan.js (score)
how_to_read: A value above 0 means the route runs through land with a protected designation. It does not say that the road is closed or that the land is off limits. In the 2026-10 snapshot the protected-areas file has seven proclamation boundaries.
caveats: The statistic for tourism places leaves out the proclamation boundaries (seven records in the 2026-10 snapshot); this route measure counts them, so the two are not on the same basis.
The file includes areas with different levels of protection and public access. The share does not tell them apart.
It is a share of sample points, not of length.
example: Snapshot 2026-10, From Río Piedras (town) To Caguas (municipality): 1%.

view.label: Map, Transit tab, Plan a route (example: Río Piedras to Caguas)

name: Municipalities crossed
plain: How many municipalities the planned route passes through. The card lists the first four names and then says 'and N more'.
definition: The number of different municipalities whose boundary contains at least one sample point of the route, with their names.
geography: Any route in Puerto Rico (calculated for the route you draw)

coverage.frequency: Recalculated in your browser each time the route changes, from the data published in the current snapshot. Resident counts are from the 2020 Census

method: plan.js finds, for each sample point, the municipality polygon that contains it and collects the distinct names. See the entry on how the route is sampled.
source_detail: municipios.geojson: TIGERweb Generalized_ACS2023 State_County MapServer layer 11 (Counties 500K, shoreline-clipped); site/js/plan.js (score)
how_to_read: Use it to see which local governments a route involves. A route that only grazes a municipality can be missed.
caveats: A municipality touched between two sample points (100 to 500 m apart) is not counted.
The boundaries follow the shoreline, so a sample point on a bridge or offshore can belong to no municipality.
The boundaries are simplified by about 22 m (0.0002 degree), so a sample point near a boundary can be assigned to the neighbouring municipality.
example: Snapshot 2026-10, From Río Piedras (town) To Caguas (municipality): 3 (San Juan, Trujillo Alto, Caguas).

view.label: Map, Transit tab, Plan a route (example: Río Piedras to Caguas)

name: Connections at the ends and stops along the route
plain: Two checks: whether the start and the end are within 300 m of a scheduled stop, and how many scheduled stops lie within 250 m of the route, by operator.
definition: Start and End: the scheduled stop nearest to the first and to the last point you chose, if one lies within 300 m in a straight line. The card shows the stop name, its operator and the distance in metres, or 'no scheduled stop within 300 m'. Existing stops within 250 m of the route: the number of scheduled stops within 250 m of the route line, grouped by operator. A scheduled stop is a stop in a public timetable feed (GTFS, the General Transit Feed Specification) from ATI (Autoridad de Transporte Integrado) or from a municipal system.
unit: stop name, operator and metres; stops per operator (count)
geography: Any route in Puerto Rico (calculated for the route you draw)

coverage.frequency: Recalculated in your browser each time the route changes, from the data published in the current snapshot. Resident counts are from the 2020 Census

method: plan.js looks at the scheduled stops in the transit features file. For the first and last chosen points it keeps the nearest stop within 300 m. For the route line it counts the stops within 250 m of the simplified line and groups them by operator's short name.
source_detail: transport.json (stops from ATI and municipal feeds); operators.json (operator names); site/js/plan.js (score, endTxt)
how_to_read: Use it to see where a new route could join an existing one. A stop near the end is a place to connect, not proof that a rider can transfer.
caveats: Only the first and last points are tested. Points you add between them are not.
Stops of operators whose timetables have expired are counted.
It does not say whether the lines at that stop go where you need, or how often.
The distance from an end is measured from the point you chose, not from the road it is snapped to.
example: Snapshot 2026-10, From Río Piedras (town) To Caguas (municipality): Start: a City of San Juan stop 50 m away. End: a Municipality of Caguas stop 51 m away. Stops within 250 m of the route: ATI 20, San Juan 29, Caguas 37. From Mayagüez (municipality) To Aguadilla (municipality): no scheduled stop within 300 m of either end.

view.label: Map, Transit tab, Plan a route (example: Río Piedras to Caguas)
Map, Transit tab, Plan a route (example with no overlap: Mayagüez to Aguadilla)

name: How the planner samples a route
plain: The flood, protected-area, overlap and municipality measures check points along the route, not the whole line. The spacing depends on the route's length.
definition: The route line is simplified to a 12 m tolerance. Points are then placed along it every 100 m for routes up to 30 km, every 250 m for routes over 30 km and up to 100 km, and every 500 m for longer routes. Every straight piece of the simplified line gets at least one point. The overlap, flood and protected-area measures are each the share of sample points that meet their test, rounded to a whole percent. The municipalities measure is the number of different municipalities that contain at least one sample point.
geography: Any route in Puerto Rico (calculated for the route you draw)

coverage.frequency: Recalculated in your browser each time the route changes, from the data published in the current snapshot. Resident counts are from the 2020 Census

method: plan.js applies Douglas-Peucker simplification (a method that drops points that lie close to a straight line between their neighbours) with a 12 m tolerance, then calls samples() with a step of 100, 250 or 500 m chosen from the route length.
source_detail: site/js/plan.js (simplifyLine, samples, score)
how_to_read: A percentage is a share of points, not a share of kilometres. Short features between points can be missed.
caveats: A curvy stretch has many short pieces, each with at least one point, so it weighs a little more than a straight stretch of the same length.
Residents, tourism places and stops use the distance to the line, not these points.

name: Planned route download (GeoJSON)
plain: The GeoJSON button saves the planned route as planned_route.geojson. The file holds the line, the points you chose and six of the results shown.
definition: A GeoJSON file (a standard text format for map shapes) with one line feature (the route) and one point feature for each chosen point. The line has the properties name, created, source, follows_roads, length_km, stops, residents_within_400m, tourism_places_within_400m, share_parallel_to_existing_routes_pct, share_in_flood_hazard_area_pct and municipalities. Each point has name, order and role.
geography: Any route in Puerto Rico (calculated for the route you draw)

coverage.frequency: Created in your browser when you press the GeoJSON button; nothing is stored on a server

method: plan.js builds the file from the current result. Coordinates are longitude and latitude (World Geodetic System 1984, WGS 84). A line that follows roads has 5 decimals; points have 6.
source_detail: site/js/plan.js (geojson, download)
how_to_read: Open the file in a mapping program to keep or share a plan. The numbers are those shown when you pressed the button.
caveats: Not in the file: the running time, residents with no scheduled stop, lodgings, the protected-area share and the connections.
'created' is the date in UTC (Coordinated Universal Time), so it can be one day ahead of the date in Puerto Rico in the evening.
A number that had not finished loading when you pressed the button is left out of the file.
The file carries the data licenses of its inputs (OpenStreetMap roads, Overture places, FEMA, Census and timetable feeds). Check the terms of each before you publish it.
The file holds the points you chose to 6 decimals (about 0.1 m) with their labels. If you chose a home address, the file shows it. Remove it before you share the file.

values.name: 'Planned route' for the line; the place label for a point.
values.created: Date the file was made, as YYYY-MM-DD in UTC.
values.follows_roads: true when Follow roads is on and every leg follows roads; false otherwise.
values.length_km: Route length in km with two decimals (the number in the 'Route length' entry).
values.stops: Labels of the chosen points joined with ' > '.
values.residents_within_400m: Residents within 400 m of the route.
values.tourism_places_within_400m: Tourism places within 400 m of the route.
values.share_parallel_to_existing_routes_pct: Share of the route within 150 m of an existing route (percent).
values.share_in_flood_hazard_area_pct: Share of the route in a flood hazard area (percent).
values.municipalities: Names of the municipalities crossed, joined with ', '.
values.order: Position of the point along the route, from 1.
values.role: 'from' for the first point, 'to' for the last, 'stop' for points between.

name: Distances used by the planner and the Transit tab
plain: The route planner and the Transit tab use a few fixed distances, all in a straight line: 150, 250, 300, 400, 500 and 800 metres. This entry says what each is for.
definition: Each distance is a setting chosen for this tool. 400 m (about a quarter mile) is a common rule of thumb for walking access to a stop. Check any agency's or programme's own definition before comparing. All are straight-line distances calculated with a flat-earth approximation, not walking distances along streets.
geography: Any route in Puerto Rico (calculated for the route you draw)

coverage.frequency: Recalculated in your browser each time the route changes, from the data published in the current snapshot. Resident counts are from the 2020 Census

method: The route planner (plan.js) and the road router (roads.js) compute distances in the browser from longitude and latitude with a flat-earth approximation: 111,320 m per degree of longitude at the equator, scaled by the cosine of the latitude, and 110,574 m per degree of latitude. The distance from each census block to its nearest scheduled stop (the basis of the 400 m and 800 m rules) and the 250 m integration-point test are computed at build time by network.py with a similar formula: 111,320 m per degree of latitude, and the same figure scaled by the cosine of the latitude for longitude. North-south distances in the build are therefore up to about 0.7% longer than in the browser. network.js and plan.js read those stored results: network.js applies the 800 m test to them and plan.js applies the 400 m test when it counts residents with no stop near a route.
source_detail: site/js/plan.js, site/js/network.js, network.py (WALK_M = 400, TRANSFER_M = 250), roads.js
how_to_read: Read each distance as a catchment around a line or a stop. A longer distance includes more people and places and says less about how easy it is to reach them.
caveats: A straight line ignores rivers, hills, fences and the street pattern.
The 400 m walking distance is about a quarter mile. The 800 m distance for service gaps is about half a mile.

values.12 m: Tolerance for simplifying the route line before it is measured.
values.100 m, 250 m, 500 m: Spacing of sample points along the route: up to 30 km, over 30 up to 100 km, over 100 km.
values.150 m: A route 'runs alongside' an existing route when a published line is within 150 m of a sample point.
values.250 m: Scheduled stops within 250 m of the route are counted. Stops of two operators within 250 m of each other make an integration point.
values.300 m: Connections at the ends: the nearest scheduled stop to the first or last point, if within 300 m.
values.400 m: Residents and tourism places counted near the route. Residents counted as served when a scheduled stop is within 400 m. The test for 'no scheduled stop within 400 m'.
values.500 m: Snap radius from a chosen point to a road.
values.800 m: Service gap: a block whose nearest scheduled stop is more than 800 m away.

name: Residents within 400 m of a scheduled stop
plain: The share of Puerto Rico's residents who live within 400 m of a stop in a public timetable. In the data of 2026-10-02 the Transit tab shows 28%, or 22% when only unexpired timetables count.
definition: Residents (2020 Census) in census blocks whose nearest scheduled stop is 400 m or less away, divided by all residents in blocks. The second figure counts a block only when a stop of an operator whose timetable has not expired lies within 400 m. A scheduled stop is a stop in a public timetable feed (GTFS, the General Transit Feed Specification) from ATI (Autoridad de Transporte Integrado) or from a municipal system.
geography: Puerto Rico, from the 36,570 census blocks that have residents (2020 Census); also stored for each municipality

coverage.frequency: Rewritten by each full build and by a nightly transit refresh that finds a changed feed (last write: 2026-10-02); the browser calculates the shares when the page opens

method: network.py measures the straight-line distance from each block's internal point to the nearest scheduled stop. It adds the residents of blocks within 400 m, overall and for blocks near a stop of an operator that is not expired. The Transit tab divides the island totals.
source_detail: network.py (coverage, WALK_M = 400); operators.json 'coverage'; site/js/network.js (renderNetSummary)
how_to_read: It says how many people have a stop near their block. It does not say how often vehicles come, where they go, or whether people can reach the stop on foot. In the data of 2026-10-02: 925,788 of 3,285,874 residents, or 28.2%, live within 400 m of a scheduled stop, and 729,507 residents, or 22.2%, live within 400 m of a stop of an operator whose timetable has not expired.
caveats: Straight-line distance, not walking distance.
A stop is a place in a timetable feed. It says nothing about frequency or hours of service.
Residents are the 2020 Census counts, assigned to each block's internal point.
Routes mapped only in OpenStreetMap (públicos) have no stops here, so no resident is counted as served by them.

In the data of 2026-10-02, fifteen municipal systems and the públicos authority report to the federal transit database but publish no timetable feed, so the people they serve count as unserved here. Do not rank municipalities on this figure without checking whether their operator publishes a feed.
The first figure includes stops of operators whose timetables have expired.

In the data of 2026-10-02, of all residents 28% are within 400 m of a stop, 60% are more than 800 m from every stop, and the other 11% (373,960 residents) are 400 to 800 m away. The shares are rounded.

view.label: Map, Transit tab: summary figures

name: Residents far from service (service-gap rule)
plain: Residents who live more than 800 m from any scheduled stop. The Transit tab shows the total and draws circles for blocks with 40 or more residents.
definition: The total residents in census blocks whose nearest scheduled stop, of any operator, is more than 800 m away (straight line), and that total as a share of all residents. Blocks with at least 40 residents are drawn as circles. A circle's radius is 2 + 0.45 times the square root of the residents, up to 14 pixels.

coverage.frequency: Rewritten by each full build and by a nightly transit refresh that finds a changed feed (last write: 2026-10-02); the browser calculates the shares when the page opens

method: network.js reads population_blocks.json, adds the residents of blocks whose distance field is above 800, and draws the blocks with 40 or more residents. The distance field is capped at 9,999 m.
source_detail: population_blocks.json (network.py, coverage); site/js/network.js (setGaps)
how_to_read: Larger circles mean more residents far from a stop. The total counts people who live more than 800 m, in a straight line, from any scheduled stop. In the data of 2026-10-02: 1,986,126 residents (60% of 3,285,874) live more than 800 m from a scheduled stop. 12,790 blocks are drawn. 9,808 further blocks with fewer than 40 residents are in the total but not drawn.
caveats: Stops from expired timetables still count as stops, so the real gaps are larger.
800 m is a distance this tool chose (about half a mile), not an official standard. Check any agency's own definition before comparing.
Straight-line distance. A stop 700 m away in a straight line can be far by road.
Residents are the 2020 Census counts, assigned to each census block's internal point.

In the data of 2026-10-02, fifteen municipal systems and the públicos authority report to the federal transit database but publish no timetable feed, so the people they serve count as far from service here. Do not rank municipalities on this figure without checking whether their operator publishes a feed.

In the data of 2026-10-02, the 60% counts residents more than 800 m from a stop. A further 11% (373,960 residents) live 37 to 800 m from a stop and are not in it. It is not the share of residents without transport.

name: Integration points
plain: Places where a stop of one transit system lies within 250 m of a stop of another system. They are natural places to coordinate timetables, fares and signs.
definition: Places where scheduled stops of two different operators are 250 m or less apart (straight line). To avoid near-duplicates, the build keeps one pair for each pair of operators in each 0.001-degree cell (about 110 m) of the first stop. One marker is drawn for each kept pair, halfway between its two stops. The map draws at most the 600 closest.

coverage.frequency: Rewritten by each full build and by a nightly transit refresh that finds a changed feed (last write: 2026-10-02)

method: network.py (transfers) compares every scheduled stop with the stops near it, keeps pairs of different operators within 250 m, keeps one pair for each pair of operators and each 0.001-degree cell (about 110 m) of the first stop, sorts by distance and stores the 600 closest with the total (counted after the thinning).
source_detail: operators.json 'transfers' and 'transfers_total' (network.py, transfers); site/js/network.js (setXfer)
how_to_read: Each marker names the two stops and their distance. It marks a candidate for coordination, not a transfer riders can make today. In the data of 2026-10-02 there are 366 such places (1,336 pairs of stops are within 250 m before this thinning), and all 366 are drawn.
caveats: Nothing checks that the routes at the two stops connect, that their times match, or that there is a safe crossing between the stops.
Stops of operators whose timetables have expired are included.
Only timetable stops count. Stops from OpenStreetMap are not included.
Two stops of the same operator never make a pair.

view.label: Map, Transit tab: Integration points

name: Vehicles on their timetable now
plain: How many trips are in progress right now according to the published timetables. It is a schedule calculation, not GPS (Global Positioning System) tracking. The Transit tab says real-time bus positions are not available to the public (checked 45-10-02).
definition: The number of trips in progress at this moment on the published timetables. The page picks the weekday, Saturday or Sunday timetable file for today's day in Puerto Rico. A trip counts when its first stop time is at or before the current time, its last stop time is at or after it, and its operator's timetable has not expired. Each dot is placed along the trip's route line, between the two timed stops the trip is between, in proportion to distance.
geography: Puerto Rico, operators with a timetable feed

coverage.frequency: Recalculated every 5 seconds in your browser while the layer is on

method: network.js picks trips.json on a weekday, trips_sa.json on Saturday or trips_su.json on Sunday, takes the time of day in Puerto Rico, keeps the trips running at that time, and places each trip along its route line between its stops (tripPoints in common.js). The weekday file holds each feed's typical weekday: Wednesday, or the first of Tuesday, Thursday, Monday or Friday that the feed serves.
source_detail: trips.json, trips_sa.json, trips_su.json (network.py); site/js/network.js (updateNow)
how_to_read: Dots show where vehicles should be if they follow the timetable. The count changes with the hour and the day.
caveats: It is a timetable, not a position. Late or cancelled trips, breakdowns and holidays are not modelled.

Timetables of expired operators are left out: in the data of 2026-10-02, 372 of the 3,297 weekday trips and 48 of the 1,648 Saturday trips. Routes whose feed lists stops out of order are left out of the timetable files. In the data of 2026-10-02, five such routes (15 weekday trips) still show trip counts in their pop-ups and in the Operators list, so a route can show trips but have no moving dots.
The weekday count uses each feed's Wednesday service for every weekday, or, if a feed has no Wednesday service, the first of Tuesday, Thursday, Monday or Friday that it serves.

In the data of 2026-10-02, on Saturday only 4 operators have trips in the timetable files (3 once the expired one is dropped), and on Sunday only ATI (Autoridad de Transporte Integrado). A system with no dots on a weekend may simply publish no weekend timetable.
Times are matched to the clock within one day. A trip that continued past midnight would not carry over into the next day. In the files of 2026-10-02 none does: the latest stop time is 24:00.

Dots follow the route line between stops at an even speed. In the 2026-10 snapshot, 106 of the 3,297 weekday trips have no line that fits their stops; their dots move in a straight line and can sit off the street.
Each timetable trip counts once. The number is not a count of physical vehicles.

name: Operators by state of their public schedule
plain: How many transit operators publish a schedule, and whether it is current, about to expire or expired. On 2026-10-02, 25 operators publish a schedule and 16 publish none. The other 3 are two that run inside the feed of the Autoridad de Transporte Integrado (ATI) and one group of routes mapped by volunteers.
definition: The operators listed are Puerto Rico agencies in the federal National Transit Database (municipal systems, the Autoridad Metropolitana de Autobuses (AMA, the Metropolitan Bus Authority), the Puerto Rico Highway and Transportation Authority (públicos) and the Puerto Rico Maritime Transport Authority (ferries)), ATI (Autoridad de Transporte Integrado), and one group for routes that volunteers mapped in OpenStreetMap. An operator with a feed has a status from the end date of its feed compared with today's date in Puerto Rico. The others have a fixed status ('No public feed', 'In the ATI feed' or 'Community-mapped'). 'Publish a schedule' means the status is current, expiring or expired.

coverage.frequency: Counts are rewritten at each full build and by a nightly refresh that finds a changed feed; the browser works out each operator's status again from its feed end date when the page opens

method: network.py reads each operator's feed and takes the last service date in its calendar (or the feed's own end date when there is no calendar). site/js/network.js (opStatus) compares it with today's date in Puerto Rico: expired when the date has passed, expiring when 60 days or fewer remain, current otherwise.
source_detail: operators.json (feed.status, feed.end); network.py (feed_status, discover); site/js/network.js (opStatus, renderNetSummary)
how_to_read: As of the build on 2026-10-02 the tab said 'operators publish a schedule (17 current, 1 expiring, 7 expired)'. The tab recalculates the split from today's date in Puerto Rico, so it changes as feeds pass their end date. A current status means the timetable's dates cover today, not that service runs as planned. The file of 2026-10-02 lists 44 operators.
caveats: Expiry is judged from one date in the feed. A feed can be out of date in practice while its end date is still ahead.
An operator with no feed may still run service. 'No public feed' says no timetable data were found, not that there is no service.
The operators come from the federal National Transit Database checklist, ATI's feed and OpenStreetMap. An operator in none of them is not listed.

values.current: On 2026-10-02: 17 operators. The last service date is more than 60 days away ('Current').
values.expiring: On 2026-10-02: 1 operator. The last service date is today or up to 60 days away ('Expires soon').
values.expired: On 2026-10-02: 7 operators. The last service date has passed ('Expired').
values.none: On 2026-10-02: 16 operators. They report to the National Transit Database but no public timetable feed was found ('No public feed').
values.in_ati: On 2026-10-02: 2 operators. The AMA buses and the Maritime Transport Authority ferries run inside the ATI feed ('In the ATI feed').
values.community: On 2026-10-02: 1 group. Routes that volunteers mapped in OpenStreetMap; no timetable ('Community-mapped').
values.broken: On 2026-10-02: 0 operators. A feed was found but could not be read ('Feed error').
values.unknown: On 2026-10-02: 0 operators. A feed was read but has no end date ('Dates unknown').

name: Routes on the map
plain: In the file of 2026-10-02 the map has 165 transit routes: 149 come from public timetable feeds and volunteers mapped 16 in OpenStreetMap.
definition: The count of route lines in the published routes file: all operators with a feed, plus the routes of the volunteer-mapped OpenStreetMap group. The Transit tab shows the count as 'routes on the map'.

coverage.frequency: Rewritten by each full build and by a nightly transit refresh that finds a changed feed (last write: 2026-10-02)

method: network.py counts the routes it writes to the routes file. Routes in a feed without a shape or stops are not drawn and not counted. The Transit tab reads the count from meta.json.
source_detail: meta.json 'network.routes'; transit_routes.geojson; site/js/network.js (renderNetSummary)
how_to_read: It counts routes, not the trips on them. One route can have two drawn lines, one for each direction.
caveats: The routes that volunteers mapped in OpenStreetMap have no timetable, so they are not scheduled service.

name: Catalog (catalog.json)
plain: The small file the map reads first, and the three it reads on first use. catalog.json holds the fields (domains) of the registry, a headline figure and trend for each, and the size of every published file; catalog_index.json holds an index of everything the dictionary documents, catalog_es.json the words of the Spanish summaries, for searching in Spanish, and catalog_views.json the ready-made views of each topic.
definition: catalog.json holds: version; built (the build time of the data, equal to meta.generated_at); snapshot (the label); domains (every domain of the registry with its Spanish and English names and descriptions, icon, accent, status, example questions, the number of dictionary entries, the number of wanted datasets by status and, for the fields that have one, a headline figure with its value, year, unit, period, trend and the way it goes on the map); and weights (the raw and the compressed size of every published file, an estimate). catalog_index.json holds the version and the build time, and: index (one row for each dictionary entry, as a list of column names and a list of rows: id, name, domain, domains, kind, geography levels, years covered, timeline, sources, the strictest license class among the sources, how the entry goes on the map and the words people use to ask for it); and sources (the data sources behind the index, with their license class). catalog_es.json holds the version and the build time, and words_es (for each entry that has a Spanish summary, the words of that summary as the page searches them: without accents, in lower case, each once, without words of one or two letters or common little words). catalog_views.json holds the version and the build time, and presets (for each topic that has them, its ready-made views: id, name and note in Spanish and English, the datasets with how each is drawn, the layers switched on, and the ids of the data sources).
geography: Whole observatory (not geographic); the headline figures are for Puerto Rico as a whole

coverage.frequency: Rebuilt with each snapshot (python catalog.py, run by build.py after the dictionary). The nightly transit refresh does not rewrite it.

method: catalog.py builds the four files from dictionary_src/domains.json, site/data/dictionary.json, the series files (housing_series.json and economy_series.json), municipalities.json, wanted.json, meta.json and the sizes of the files in site/data. python catalog.py --check says whether the files on disk are current; it ignores the build time and the sizes. Compressed sizes are an estimate (gzip, level 6) of what a web server sends. The index is a file of its own so the map's first load stays small (docs/performance.md).
source_detail: catalog.py (build, headline, island_value, build_index, map_action, weights); the sources are those of the figures named in methods.headline_figures
how_to_read: Read a headline figure as the number for the whole island over the period it names. The index lets a page find data without loading the whole dictionary (about 2.4 MB). The weights tell a visitor what a module costs before it loads.
caveats: A headline figure is not a score and the fields are not comparable with one another. See methods.headline_figures for how each is worked out and what it counts.

The license class in the index is the strictest class among an entry's sources. It describes the sources as recorded in the sources list, not a legal review, and it can be strict for an entry that only cites a study (for example, an entry that cites a study with no stated license is marked 'license not stated').

How an entry goes on the map is read from where the entry says its data live (a yearly series file, a field of municipalities.json) or, for a layer, from the list in dictionary_src/map_layers.json. Entries with neither have no 'Add to map' button.
The sizes are estimates, and they can lag the files until catalog.py runs again (for example after the nightly transit refresh).

values.domains: One object for each domain of the registry, system domains included (they are left out of the overview).
values.index: In catalog_index.json. {fields: [...], rows: [[...], ...]}. One row for each dictionary entry; the column 'map' is how it goes on the map: ['econ', dataset key] or ['econ', dataset key, scale], ['layers', layer keys] or none.
values.sources: In catalog_index.json. The data sources behind the index, with their license class. Base maps, libraries and tools are left out.
values.weights: {file name: {raw, gz}} in bytes for every published file except the four catalog files.
values.presets: In catalog_views.json. {topic id: [ready-made views]}; each view {id, name, note, show: [[dataset key, 'fill' or 'symbol', {norm: its scale, ramp: its colours}]], on: [layer keys], sources: [source ids]}. A view replaces what is on the map.
values.words_es: In catalog_es.json. {entry id: the words of its Spanish summary, separated by spaces}, for the entries that have a Spanish summary.
